paper_title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: System-1 Decision Models make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given textual state in single forward pass (TypeSafe AI, 2026; Microsoft, 2026), which support diverse applications, including text and intent classification, model and tool selection, and rubric-based 1 quality scoring (Ling et al., 2026). Therefore, rigorous and comprehensive evaluation of these models must account for the diversity and complexities of decision making in real-world scenarios. Recent benchmarks have assessed decision models across diverse tasks and calibration criteria (Duan et al., 2026; Solka, 2026; Standhartinger, 2026). However, many existing evaluations draw heavily on widely circulated public benchmarks, making test-set contamination central concern for benchmark validity (Oren et al., 2024). Moreover, real-world decisions often combine long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies. For example, practically useful model needs to track the current agent state, determine whether an earlier approval remains valid, and select an eligible tool from large catalog with heterogeneous prerequisites. These settings call for an evaluation that combines task breadth with new instances and explicit tests of these capabilities. In this paper, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), benchmark of 5,448 questions for evaluating text-based System-1 Decision Models across realistic decision scenarios. It combines broad task coverage with explicit tests of context understanding, option discrimination, and logical consistency. Table 1 compares its scope with existing decision benchmarks. Specifically, MMDM evaluates Hard Singleselect, Hard Multi-select, and Soft-label questions, requiring unique correct choice, the complete valid set, or prediction matching the reference distribution over outcomes. These answer types capture practical requirements such as choosing the next actions, identifying all eligible tools, and assigning probabilities to rubric scores under uncertainty. Decisions can depend on agent states, action prerequisites, or relationships among options. In benchmark construction, source answers and contextual evidence ground rewrites of states, queries and distractors to reduce memorizationinduced score inflation (Zhu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). We combine these adaptations with recompositions and newly constructed tasks. The resulting 16 categories span knowledge and comprehension, logic and constraints, agent and workflow decisions, and preference and rubric judgments. With 21,024 options and complete inputs of up to 64,817 tokens, MMDM also tests these capabilities across varied context lengths and option spaces. As shown in Figure 1, our evaluation of 28 decision models reveals substantial differences across capabilities. Models that perform well on world knowledge still struggle with interdependent options, decisions subject to constraints, and complete multi-select recovery. These capabilities matter in agent workflows, where choices interact, actions have prerequisites, and several tools or skills may be valid for the current goal. Specifically, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 (Perplexity AI, 2026) achieves 78.75% Hard Single-select accuracy on world knowledge, compared with 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning. WeMM-JEV 27B (WeMM-JEV Team, 2026) achieves the highest Hard Single-select accuracy of 76.00%, while the highest Hard Multi-select accuracy is 36.81%, highlighting the challenge of recovering all valid options. Model rankings also differ between hardanswer accuracy and soft-distribution error, making both necessary to characterize decision quality. Overall, our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce multitask decision benchmark that combines fresh decision instances with long contexts, large option spaces, and interdependent options. Second, we provide unified evaluation protocol for single-select correctness, multi-select completeness, and soft-label distributional fidelity, together with an open dataset and toolkit. Third, our evaluation reveals capability gaps that are not captured by previous decision-model benchmarks, including failures in joint consistency and complete multi-select recovery, providing concrete directions for future model development.

sections.title: 3.2 Data Collection and Construction
sections.content: Collection. We select public datasets and agent trajectories that support concrete decision with explicit options and checkable answer. Sources span knowledge, reading, reasoning, preferences, code, and agent interactions. For example, QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) and LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) supply document-grounded questions, BIRD (Li et al., 2023) supplies database problems, and ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025) and ToolTalk (Farn and Shin, 2023) supply interaction histories. Source questions and annotations provide the basis for adaptation and verification. Construction. We combine source-grounded adaptation with semantic recomposition and newly constructed tasks. For rewritten source instances, we retain the original answers and supporting evidence while reformulating the state, query, and distractors. Semantic and option-quality checks select the resulting instances. This strategy builds on evidence that benchmark rewriting can mitigate memorization-induced score inflation (Zhu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). Recompositions introduce decision questions grounded in source databases or agent histories. Executable mechanisms construct interacting options, constrained plans, state transitions, and rubric outcomes with computable answers. Across all three routes, distractors are designed around identifiable failure modes, such as applying an expired rule, confusing entities, or overlooking the prerequisite. Validation and Selection. We verify answers using source evidence, executable checks, and model review appropriate to each construction route. Fivemodel majority screening is followed by independent human expert review of borderline cases. Both stages apply the same quality standards for distractors, answer leakage, duplicates, and source overlap. An option-only probe masks the state and query; instances with unresolved shortcuts are excluded. Appendix details the review procedure and selection rules.

sections.title: 3.3 Task Coverage and Dataset Statistics
sections.content: MMDM contains 5,448 questions across 16 task categories, comprising 4,112 Hard Single-select, 633 Hard Multi-select, and 703 Soft-label questions. The 663 Score questions include 35 with hard levels and 628 with soft targets. The collection covers 62 registered source identifiers and 80 categorysubcategory combinations. Option sets range from 2 to 1,024 options, including 94 questions with more than 255 options. Complete inputs include the state, query, option names, and criteria. We measure complete inputs with the Qwen3.54B tokenizer from the Qwen family (Yang et al., 2025). Their median length is 827 tokens, the 95th percentile is 13,318, and the maximum is 64,817. These ranges support evaluation from common short decisions to long-document reasoning and large-catalog selection. The categories connect knowledge and language understanding with decisions about evidence, rules, Figure 2: Task coverage and answer semantics. The colors of the 16 task categories are fixed across figures. Labels show the total count followed by (Hard Singleselect / Hard Multi-select / Soft-label) counts. actions, and assessments. They cover world knowledge and reading comprehension; deductive, quantitative, and option-dependent reasoning; agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, and workflows; and preference, rubric, and emotion judgments. sections.content: Model rankings change between long inputs and large option sets. The two panels of Figure 4 reveal different scaling profiles. MMDM measures both axes because success on one does not predict the model ordering on the other. Large catalogs expose differences hidden by compact choices. In Figure 4, Jev and Microsoft Decision-1 differ by about seven percentage points on 24 options, but by more than 37 points on 1291,024 options. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced MMDM, benchmark of 5,448 questions across 16 task categories for evaluating text-based System-1 Decision Models. With option sets ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs reaching approximately 64K tokens, MMDM tests decisions across both familiar requests and complex contexts. Its single-select, multi-select, and soft-label tasks assess whether models choose correctly, identify all valid options, and assign useful probabilities and scores. Our evaluation of 28 decision models reveals clear gaps between these capabilities and exposes dimensions of decision quality that are not captured by previous benchmarks. The strongest models vary across answer types and task categories. High single-select accuracy can accompany inaccurate probabilities, while deduction and routing strengths coexist with weaknesses in joint constraints and workflow decisions. Reliability curves and scaling profiles further distinguish confidence quality from accuracy and long-input performance from large-option performance. These findings direct progress toward checking interacting conditions, handling larger decision spaces, and producing probabilities that support reliable choices and scores. We release MMDM and its evaluation toolkit to make progress on these capabilities easy to measure and compare.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: MMDM has three main limitations. First, it focuses on text-based decisions defined by fixed state, query, and option set. Extending MMDM to multimodal inputs and interactive trajectories would broaden its coverage of real-world decision settings. Second, multi-select questions are concentrated in option logic, constraint planning, workflows, and tool or skill selection, while most soft targets come from rubric scoring. These settings provide clear labels and verifiable target distributions, but broader evaluation of subjective judgments will require references that better capture variation across human assessments. Third, MMDM combines newly constructed tasks with source-preserving adaptations, recompositions, and rewrites. Although recompositions and rewrites introduce new decision requirements and contexts, prior exposure to the underlying public source material may still occur.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: MMDM combines publicly available research data with newly constructed decision tasks. We cite the source datasets and document their contributions in Appendix B. Source materials remain subject to their original terms of use. The same appendix describes model-assisted construction, label verification, and targeted human review, including independent assessment and adjudication of disagreements. Our experiments evaluate model predictions from recorded or simulated inputs; they do not execute the tools or workflows described in the questions. We release the benchmark and evaluation toolkit, with source attribution, to support transparent and reproducible research.

sections.title: A Input Coverage and Task Definitions
sections.content: Classification and Coverage. Table A1 defines the 16 capabilities and links each one to its corresponding example in Appendix F. category identifies the capability decision requires; the answer type specifies whether the target is one option, complete valid set, or distribution. We measure input length using the full text seen by the model, including the state, query, option names, and option criteria. Each example is capped at 65,535 tokens. Among the 5,448 examples, 3,155 are shorter than 1K tokens, while 356 exceed 8K tokens, including 107 longer than 32K. The number of options ranges from 2 to 1,024. At inference time, the actual token usage can be slightly higher because model providers add their own request formatting and reserved tokens. Decision Interfaces. Jev exposes three interfaces for different kinds of requests (TypeSafe AI, 2026). They specify what the model returns. The answer types in Section 3.1 specify what makes prediction correct and how it is evaluated. Choice compares named options. support request might ask whether ticket belongs to billing, shipping, or returns, with each options criterion defining its responsibilities. The response contains the selected option and probability for every option. In MMDM, this distribution supports evaluation against single correct option, set of equally valid options, or soft reference, according to the tasks answer type. Noul answers yes/no query, such as whether message requests refund. It returns the probability of yes; values near one favor yes, values near zero favor no, and values near one-half express uncertainty between them. The remaining probability belongs to no, giving the two-option distribution used in evaluation. definite reference answer is hard single-select, while reference that quantifies uncertainty is soft-label. Score evaluates an input against ordered, descriptive rubric levels. For report completeness, these might range from missing required evidence to meeting every requirement. The response contains probability for each level and their probabilityweighted numeric score. MMDM evaluates both the level distribution and the expected score. Therefore, Scoring questions belong to the hard singleselect or soft-label track, depending on whether the reference identifies one level or distribution.

OpenJev answers all 55 high-confidence SQL questions correctly, compared with 63.2% of its 38 high-confidence emotion questions. Thus, the same confidence threshold corresponds to different error rates across tasks. To capture this variation, we compute ECE separately within each task category using the same ten confidence bins, then weight the results by question count. This prevents overconfidence in one task from cancelling underconfidence in another. ECE rises from 0.054 to 0.106 for Jev, from 0.085 to 0.110 for Intern-Decision, and from 0.092 to 0.116 for OpenJev. Jev illustrates the opposing errors, with confidence exceeding accuracy by 38.6% on Emotion Recognition but falling below it by 29.0% on Workflow Decision. Expected Scores and Their Distributions. We examine 596 sampled-rubric questions using native predictions from all five models on complete inputs. For predictions with nMAE at most 0.05, equivalent to an error of at most 0.2 points on the 04 scale, we measure distribution error using total (cid:80) variation, TV(p, π) = 1 pj πj. This is the 2 probability mass that must be reassigned to match the reference. Jev meets this nMAE threshold on 190 questions and Intern-Decision on 111. Their mean TV errors remain 0.323 and 0.306, respectively. Thus, close estimate of the expected score can still misrepresent the probabilities of individual score levels. Each question scores random subset of records against four criteria. The expected total score depends on the four individual pass probabilities, while the full score distribution also depends on which criteria pass together. Using the exact pass probabilities, we construct an approximation that treats the criteria as independent. It preserves the expected score but produces mean Brier and TV errors of 0.0127 and 0.0690 across the 596 questions. This illustrates why accurate expected scores and accurate score distributions require different information.
